BH army documents show that even the cease-fire that we signed was violated by them and that they wanted the events to unfold in such a way that we were completely cut off in Vakuf and to prepare for an attack on Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise again, Mr. President, if I could just ask for one follow-up clarification. There are no blue HVO positions indicated on the Makljen feature. And is the witness testifying that the HVO was not holding the Makljen feature at that time? I may be missing it, but I don't see any HVO positions indicated in the area of Makljen ridge. So if he could clarify that, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Praljak, why is there this arrow pointing towards the Makljen ridge when there is no presence of HVO in Makljen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO was at Makljen, but it's not marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were soldiers in Makljen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not soldiers. There was a check-point, a police check-point, at Makljen. There was no need for the troops to be stationed at Makljen, but cutting Makljen off and taking this check-point in effect would have caused the whole situation in Prozor to fall through. So had the Neretvica Brigade managed to do that, the military situation would have been very bleak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. General Praljak, I will not show you any documents for paragraph 95 and 99. But this deals with Mostar. You say that after July 24th, 1993, you were very rarely in Mostar because the headquarters were in Citluk at the time. Therefore, you had no direct knowledge about events in Mostar in 1993, that you were never informed about any alleged crimes that would have been committed in Mostar. This is what's written in paragraph 95. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm this. I inspected some positions once during that time. However, since I knew that without taking Vakuf and Rama the Mostar offensive would probably fall through, I believe that our position in Mostar was such that it would become critical only if we lost Vakuf and Prozor, which both Mr. Petkovic and I knew as well as Mr. Tole, that's why I focused on the areas of Prozor and Vakuf. Having said that I would like to say that on the 15th of August and then in the fighting in Vrde when they tried to break through, of course I was engaged there as well, and when they made an attempt in the direction of south, I would come for a day or two. It's very difficult to go back in time and reconstruct exactly what was going on. But as for this information, I did not have any such information. I only had military reports. That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding Mostar, on paragraph 99 it says that on May 11th, at a check-point, there was a problem with a soldier from the SpaBat who had been wounded and that you actually intervened at that time. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your counsels say that at that time you had no formal authority over the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is correct, of course, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On paragraph 101, this is an important date for you, June 30th, 1993, you say that there was a mutiny of Muslim soldiers within the HVO units. Could you -- didn't your intelligence people -- hadn't they told you about the possibility of this mutiny? You couldn't have -- weren't you expecting it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not have any duties and -- in the HVO at the time. On that particular date I was a foot soldier in Boksevica and I've already described this very well. Maybe up to the 10th of July, 1993, that was the case. I don't know what they were supposed to have and how much they had. I learned this from Mr. Siljeg. And this was not only in Mostar and Stolac, that was also in Livno in part, and so on and so forth. As a foot soldier on the front line in Boksevica, but irrespective of having been a soldier and for later having been the commander for the liberation of Boksevica by Mr. Petkovic, my influence on the people who remained there was significant. I was a soldier, but when I said that I am not leaving Boksevica, they were exhausted and frustrated but they stayed with me. One has to spell things out very precisely is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 105 there is mention of the siege of Mostar. There is a dispute on the siege of Mostar. In this submission it seems to say that there was no siege of Mostar because eastern Mostar was controlled by the ABiH, there was communication, and even though there were no first-class roads or even highways they could still use smaller roads. You even say that there was a passage adjacent to the Bijela bridge north from Mostar. So first let's talk about the term "siege." When you mention the siege of Mostar, some people get the impression that it's like Stalingrad or Vukovar. As far as you're concerned, was this a siege in the military sense of the word or was it just a problematic situation that was not a siege per se? It seems to be what you develop in paragraph 107.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostar was never under siege in either military or in any other terms. Communication between Mostar and Jablanica via the road route across the Bijela bridge existed and could be used and the BH army did that until the moment they themselves, probably afraid that the population would flee, they themselves destroyed it by demolishing the second line in October 1993, and the first one had already been destroyed. And even then they could take the round-about way or some other way. There were all sorts of ways. Your Honours, in military terms, the HVO was from the north to the south, mostly along the Neretva River, a little bit here, a little bit there, the western part of Mostar was under the BiH army and the HVO was on the opposite side. How could one speak about the siege of Mostar, especially given the fact that you saw General Drekovic's documents and you could see that with the Serbs, they no longer had a proper defence line. They had guards and patrols from the south of Mostar all the way up to Konjic. What siege? It really doesn't make any sense at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, on paragraph 110 your counsels, probably under your control, develop a theory. They say that the ABiH had its artillery position extremely close to the military hospital, which is what you told us during the cross-examination of a number of witnesses. Then it says also that the command post of the 4th Corps of the ABiH and the command post of the 1st Brigade were in eastern Mostar, whereas before May 9th they were located in Mostar west, that there was a mixture of military and civilian, that military camouflage dress was in common use, that many people wore it, civilians sometimes could wear it, vice versa, that civilians were frequently armed. And as a conclusion, in paragraph 110, it says that it was absolutely impossible to distinguish potential targets. What can you say about this and can you give us any additional information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you've seen documents issued by the Spanish Battalion, at least ten of them. In these documents they are warning the BiH army to remove mortars away from the hospital. They did that purposefully, not only near the hospital, but on the road by the houses, between the houses in Mostar. They kept cannons there, the red arrows as well, mortars, anti-aircraft guns, and they opened fire from all of those. That's what I had to say by way -- one. Second of all, one corps had its command, the brigades have their commands, the battalions have their commands, companies have their commands. Your Honours, we're talking about at least 50 or 60 commands that were all military targets and they were all housed in Mostar among the buildings. In the main street of the eastern part of Mostar, the Marsal Tito street housed the command of the 4th Corps, the command of the military police, and so on and so forth. This was done intentionally. Despite all that, you saw information about 520 soldiers who were killed in 1993 on the side of the BiH army, General Drekovic wrote about that. If there was non-selective and excessive firing on Mostar, the number of civilians, the dead civilians, would have been at least two or three times higher than the number of fallen soldiers. You saw that the Prosecutor heard a lady who spoke about that, and this corroborates my claim that the number of killed civilians was negligible. I claim that on my order and on the order of my commanders there was a minimal number of responses to their shelling and when we did that it was selective. We never targeted or hit the hospital because I never allowed my artillery men to target their mortars which were placed there strategically and intentionally hoping that we would miss and that we would target and hit the hospital, and then the whole world would talk about the criminal HVO. None of the things contained in here are correct. I'm telling you the facts and I'm giving you the figures which are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in paragraph 125 you say that you were never informed of any incident coming from sniping. At least that's what's written in paragraph 125. Now, you're under oath and you were telling us that when you were a general commanding the HVO, from January [as interpreted] to November, you were never informed of any sniping with possible consequences, people being killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never informed about that, and I contest the thesis that sharp-shooters killed people. Based on what was shown to this Trial Chamber, this is not correct. Every case has to be proven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see a document we've already seen, 3D 1469 just a technical question on the document. This is a letter you sent to Mr. Tudjman regarding the destruction of the Old Bridge, 14th of October, 1997 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know this letter, he didn't want to see you, that's why you wrote to him, and then you said, But please, ask Miroslav Tudjman, ask Rebic and Lucic to answer the questions that follow, and then you name the questions. We know, because you told us, that Miroslav is his father's son and he was in charge of the HIS. As to Markica Rebic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he was the head of the SIS of the Croatian army. Whereas Mr. Lucic was the head of the SIS of the HVO. I don't know whether that was at the same time; however, at the time when the Old Bridge was destroyed, they were in those respective positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you thought that these three individuals had all the necessary information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was their duty to continue the investigation as to what had happened. I don't know whether they had information or not. I knew that the investigation had started and was halted and that from then on nobody seems to -- seemed to have cared that every week my name comes up in a newspaper in connection with the Old Bridge. And in vein of the Goebbels doctrine, this became a notorious fact. Here you can see that I don't entitle this letter as: Dear Mr. President. I was outraged and then I say, Sincerely, and I don't sign myself as General. I sign myself as a professor, and I don't even greet him, and I don't even share my thoughts of love and respect with him. I just say, Sincerely, Praljak, professor, not "General." I was angry. By that time what was in play was something that exists in the world today, which is broadcasting a piece of false information for 30 times and then it becomes the truth, and then all of a sudden, you have an act of classical information fascism in play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the consequences for displaced people, paragraph 144, and two documents: 1D 01198, that's the first document. You say that there were displaced people from Stolac that caused many problems in Capljina and that all this created tensions. In support of this we have two documents that we're going to have a look at. The first document is a text by Mr. Markovic, the HVO president in Stolac, regarding the rights and obligations of refugees. Why did you mention this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no clue. I would not refer to this document. This was past my time. Maybe Mr. Kovacic can answer, and if you allow me, I have to go and spend a penny on a -- I would never quote this document. It has nothing whatsoever to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I see. Go ahead. Wait a minute. There's an emergency. We'll wait for you. In the meantime, Mr. Kovacic, can you tell us why this document was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as you can see, this is just a list of all the evidence as aide-memoire, as something that helps everybody read. This is not evidence. This is just the expectation from a testimony. This is a group of documents which deals with the topic or, in other words, confirms the assertion presented in paragraph 144. And as far as I can remember, I'm not in a position to check, all it boils down to is the beginning of May 1992, and it seems to me that some of the documents have already been used on General Praljak's direct. They were on our list and all of these documents cover the year 1992. The entire topic is in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until Mr. Praljak is back in court, let's call up the second document, P 00492.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, whilst you're asking General Praljak a question, maybe you could be more precise about the time because he has no way of orientating himself in the summary. That will help him to find his bearings in the summary and answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General Praljak, regarding the displaced persons in Stolac who caused problems in Capljina, what is the time-frame, according to you, because you see a document, you don't know this document, but we see the date of December 1992 in this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document I have -- I can't talk about December 1992 in Capljina because I was in Central Bosnia at that time if I were there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know where does this confusion come from, but the document by that number bears the date 16 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a totally different kettle of fish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said there were two documents. The first document is of December 1992 by the HVO president in Stolac. The second document, which is bound to be a problem for Mr. Stringer because there is no translation into English but one in French, and the date is 16th of December, 1992. So as to the latter document, no need for a translation. It is by the Bregava Stolac Brigade. So the period is the 16th of September, 1992, before the December 1992 text, and Commander Pizovic is the author of the document. He says that the brigade was created on the 25th of August by decision of the Main Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that it received 300 volunteers who have received theoretical and practical training. And they say that they can have a company of 120 men with infantry weaponry. So this is a military document, Mr. Praljak. What is the meaning of this document for Stolac and Capljina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that the theory of joint criminal enterprise does not exist. Why would anybody who wanted to cleanse Stolac ethnically, after we returned it in the month of June 1992, why would anybody allow a brigade to be established there? And as for the training, Mr. Pizovic and his men conducted that training in western Herzegovina and partly on the coast in Croatia after the date when we transported all the refugees from Stolac, Muslims, and I was involved in that. And if you can remember my question put to the witness when I asked him whether everybody enjoyed the same rights, Muslims and Croats, and he said yes. That army was armed, the people returned and he is now informing the 1st Brigade of the HVO, the 1st Herzegovina Brigade Capljina, the command, he says to the HVO, Here you go. I have that many, give me an area that I am going to defend from now. And that brigade eventually grew to a thousand men with the weapons that we provided them with, and so on and so forth, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to possibly the most important document, P 09811. We have examined it already, but let's -- there are good reasons to have another look at it. You mentioned the document in paragraph 154 of your submissions. Your case is that you have never written the document and that you never said "show no mercy." Let's have a look at the document together. We can see that it was drafted by the duty operational officer, by Zorinko Bosnjak. It comes from the Ban Josip Zelovic [phoen] Brigade in Kiseljak, the date being the 24th of October, 1993. It is sent to the Bobovac Brigade. We can also see that there is another addressee, namely Ivica Rajic. You can see his name, can't you. So oddly enough with regard to the font it's not in the same colour as what is above, namely Vares. Normally we should have the same font. One may even wonder whether the last part was not added on later. Look at contents of the document, please. It regards information on sending of the request to the XY side. The PS part is important. So I read this and it seems that at some point in time you said that no mercy should be shown towards anybody. Now, how do you read this document personally? Let me be very clear, Mr. Praljak. Any reasonable Judge, upon reading the document, could say, Well, General Praljak tells Rajic that one should show no mercy. So you can see the conclusion that can be drawn. What can you say to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the thing is very simple. I didn't write anything to Rajic or the Bobovac Brigade or anybody there. I did not issue orders to them, to no Rajic or Bobovac Brigade ever. I wrote to General Petkovic, the original document, after I had received multiple reports about disorder in Vares, smuggling, Harah's adverse situation, there were five, seven, even more reports. It was then that I wrote General Petkovic and I wrote to him -- Petkovic, I'm not issuing him orders. I'm writing Petkovic and then the text, Put the situation in Vares in order without any mercy. In our terms that means - I would kindly ask the interpreters to be very precise - "impartially." You have to be impartial. To hell with all the relatives, brothers, sisters, neighbours, to hell with them, do it without mercy. That was the sense of the word. You know, Your Honours, you have to understand that the previous system relied on family and local ties. It was scratch my back, I'll scratch yours; however, the second part of the sentence says this and I quote almost: Find good people. Once you have dealt with the thieves, criminals, and ignoramuses without any mercy, then find people who are up to the times and up to the task; the times are the times of war and the task is to defend ourselves. And -- but Petkovic understood my letter the way it is spelled out. I meant find Croats. I'm not talking about showing no mercy towards the Muslims. I'm talking about the Muslims and -- about the Croats and their structure, and any reasonable trier of facts would understand this the way it was written. And I wrote this paper in 1993 when the situation in Stupni Do was already over and when some idiots over there thought that they could use this as if I had instructed them, then that would be a lie. However, I trust that the Judges before me are reasonable triers of facts and that they will understand. Who I sent the document to, what happened before that, when I sent the document, and what the sense and the meaning of the document is. They had to know the documents that preceded the situation over there, they had to read the first sentence, the second sentence, and they had to understand that it arises very clearly from the second sentence, that that sentence deals with putting the situation in order among the Croats themselves. I can say as much about the whole situation and now I don't have to say a word more. I really place a lot of trust in the common sense of the Judges here before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have the break soon, but before the break let's have a look at two documents related to paragraph 167 about Joint Command. The first document is P 01198. I must tell you, Mr. Praljak, that I did not quite understand why this document was being mentioned. It comes from the Ante Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf and it is sent to the IPD in Mostar on the 18th of January, 1993. What is the point in mentioning this document in your submissions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't matter to me. This document is not important to me. It's the discretionary judgement or assessment on the part of my lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move to P 01324. We've seen it already. It is the 22nd Session of the Croatian Council of Defence, 27th of January, 1993. It was a meeting with Mr. Zubak, Tomic, Soljic, et cetera. You did not attend the meeting. We see the agenda and the various decrees that are to be adopted. Why did you mention this document in relation to paragraph 167 to show the Joint Command of the BiH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The logic is entirely unclear, but Mrs. Nika is here so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is a technical error here. The footnotes got mixed up and that is the problem and we didn't check that but -- yes, the topic doesn't fit. We did have the topic "Praljak calms the situation down," but it was not in this folder, paragraph 167 of our summary pertained to -- well, it says here on the Joint Command, that's what you said. The general headline of that -- the title of that chapter was "Praljak calms the situation down." So this is a technical problem and I take my part of the blame for not checking it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a break and I'll ask the Registrar to call-up after the break 3D 03519. We'll see this document after the break. I don't know whether I will be able to finish everything today because I still have quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have a document by Mr. Pasalic, 14th of November, 1992, several days after the Prozor events obviously. This documents admits that they may be BH army and HVO units together, jointly. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made efforts at the time while I was there for the BH army units and the HVO units to take some joint actions so that they developed this feeling that they are a single army defending Bosnia and Herzegovina. One of the things that I arranged with them was for a position of the Republika Srpska army further up from Konjic, in the village of Bijela, this was the position which threatened Konjic in particular, to push them back or to take it, to liberate it, whatever term you want to use. With the BH army and the HVO commanders I personally undertook a reconnaissance mission twice. On one occasion it was a reconnaissance in force which means that there was an exchange of fire with the Republika Srpska army troops. And we agreed that we should carry out this action jointly and they had to prepare everything on my instructions and in accordance with the agreement, but we have to be really very precise here. There were quite a few people among the Muslims and BH army ranks who wanted to cooperate, but as time went by, this number decreased and they were pilloried. They were accused of collaborating with the HVO. It was tantamount to you, for instance, being accused of collaborating with Nazi Germany. Since the operation at Komar, near Travnik, fell through, they played me for a fool, they cheated me. And when I got down there to carry out this action, the BH army decided not to participate. I never found out who issued the order for them not to participate in this action with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 171 and a document, 3D 00484. It has to do with relations between the HVO and the HOS. It is a very long document. It is signed by Ante Prkacin, HOS unit commander. That's what you say in paragraph 171. Last-but-one paragraph there. Show us the end of the document, Registrar, please. In this last-but-one paragraph he seems to say that he can assist Mr. Blaskic, Mr. Kordic, and he says: "We can take 40 of my men and 40 domestic fighters." First question: Do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was down there at the time. This document, Your Honour, pertains to the document that we discussed a little while ago, the one that was signed by Bruno Stojic and myself about sending the 240 or 50 people - well, I don't know how many of them, 80 per cent of them were Muslims and they were led by Ante Prkacin, and Alija Izetbegovic publicly recognised him as a general of the BH army so he was -- well, this is what happened. This is an exhaustive report indicating that this man leading a group with 80 per cent Muslims was not allowed to get into Central Bosnia. He managed to break through with a smaller group and I worked together with him. I think I appointed him to the command at one point, the command that was charged with attempts to re-take Jajce, but this was illusory in military terms. It could never come to nothing, especially because on the BH army side there was no desire -- well, apart from these guys -- not the entire BH army, Lendo sabotaged everything; but Leko, a Muslim for Turbe, fought really valiantly, not only he, but there were some other smaller Muslim units that were requesting my assistance and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, your counsel in paragraph entitled "Specific Documents," it is paragraph 183, says that you yourself, Mr. Praljak, wanted to deal with 33 documents. I examined the documents. They can be perused very quickly, provided your comments are very short, but if your counsel wrote this down, he must have done this at your request. This is paragraph 183 and I want to be totally exhaustive. I want to deal with all facets of your defence case. We are going to look at the documents, therefore, but please be short in your comments so that we can proceed swiftly. First document, P 02526, 26th of May, 1993, a document sent by Petkovic to the Ljubuski Brigade. You are mentioned in the document under 2. Why is this document important?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why this is important, the 26th of May -- well, that's the date when probably there was some fighting with the BH army because at that time it had already started, skirmishes had already started. I was probably up there -- well, I don't know why this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second document, P 02781. Commander Ivica Lucic is sending this document to Colonel Siljeg following a conversation with General Praljak, with Petkovic, and Bruno Stojic on the 14th of June in Mostar in which they had asked to send a tank crew to Prozor. What are your reflections on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... military document and it's a weird sentence. "Understand," that's what Milivoj Petkovic is saying. Imagine a military document where it says: Please understand that Prozor and Gornji Vakuf are under threat. Well, the attacks are being launched by the BH army and the tank is being requested, it was probably being repaired, and that's why Stojic had to be asked about it, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, I think it is interesting, P 03912. This is an oral order you issued on the 3rd of August, 1993. You have it in your own language. Snipers must be sent. There are members of the snipers squad of the 2nd HVO Brigade in Mostar. Mr. Praljak, for any reasonable trier of fact this document shows that there are four individuals who are members of a sniper squad in Mostar, and it seems that these individuals are to go somewhere and they should report to General Praljak. So how do you interpret this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's proper from the military point of view. There are snipers in every army. They have sniper rifles. I can't remember at this point in time, but I don't deny that I would have issued an order of this kind if I needed four men. So there is no reason for me to challenge this order, an order of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 03971. The date is 5th of August, 1993, sent by the Prozor Rama Brigade. This document is sent to the HVO president in Prozor. It is about the issue of recruits or conscripts from 16 to 60 years of age. How do you interpret this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document signed by member of the SIS, and he hereby notifies the HVO Presidency and the brigade command that they have complied with somebody's order, an order from somebody higher up. Now, who that is, who was higher up and what the order was that they complied with, you can see it here. I don't know who the higher up -- the person higher up was who issued this order, but you should ask the chief of the SIS who ordered this. I have nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 05355. It is a document by Zlatko Ferencevic. He seems to be the commander of the 3132 military post and he's sending this to the operational zone in the north-western part of Herceg-Bosna. He says that there was reinforcement with 350 soldiers, which seems to imply the involvement of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What is your take on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this man wrote. I have never seen this document in my life and these soldiers never reached this territory, never, ever. I don't know how come that this is written here, what the origin of this whole story is, well, I don't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the next document, P 07034. This is by Mr. Siljeg, a document sent of the 24th of December, 1993. You were no longer in your position, but your name is mentioned in the document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's quite obvious that Anton Juric, who I know, who fought in Vukovar, and in 1992 he was with me down there in Capljina, Mostar, and so on, a great officer, a great fighter, and I managed to talk him into staying there. But this is not an oral order -- well, Siljeg, you know, it's a -- the request, a plea, and he remained down there and he performed this function and now it's just a certificate issued for the purposes of the Croatian army to the effect Praljak kept him here, so when you're checking of his whereabouts you can prove that he acted there as a volunteer. He had been a volunteer in 1992, he fought in Vukovar and he managed to break through, and there was another guy Brekalo, and they were born, both of them, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You might shed some light on a document that I personally did not understand very well. It is P 01194, under seal. So it is not to be broadcast. It is about the Alpha-Bravo Operation. Mention is made of Halilovic and Petkovic. There's also the issue of the ultimatum. The situation in Mostar and the situation in Jablanica. Why is this document important for your defence case and were you made aware of this document? Was it shown to you by your lawyers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have seen this document earlier. It makes no sense. It's the 17th or the 18th of the January. What is the date of this document? What -- January, the 17th? Well, they simply received it from the BH army. They got this story about the ultimatum. There was no ultimatum. There was a demand in Gornji Vakuf for them to withdraw from the heights that they had taken. That was the position of the HVO. You could call it a demand, you could call it an ultimatum. And there was no other ultimatum. There was an order of Alija Izetbegovic and his defence minister Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us that this document of an international character mentions an ultimatum but there was no such thing as an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, these are just rumours. We heard it and so on. There's a huge pile of those documents which are, to be quite honest, are completely worthless and -- well, for the most part they simply relayed the positions of the BH army without checking the veracity of their claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P 01330. This is an SIS report, 27th of January, 1993, handwritten report it is, speaking about Gornji Vakuf, about torched houses, and it also says that the HVO military police is responsible. What do you have to say to this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. If the SIS received the report, under the law which was in force at the time it has to act on the report, carry out an investigation, and bring in persons who did that and hand them over to the public prosecutor, or rather, the military prosecutor and the court to be prosecuted. That was their duty. It was their fundamental duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document mentioned by you, P 05330. You have to compare this document with other documents about detainees taken out of Heliodrom to -- for them to work outside. So we have a pre-printed form and names and dates just put in. This is a document of the 23rd of September, 1993, when you were HVO commander. We see that there are 30 detainees that left Heliodrom. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you are following the summary, then P 05530 is the next document, and the record shows that you asked for 5330 and that's the document we have on our screen. And in the summary it's not 5330 but 5530. So if you're following the list, I believe you are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Well, perchance we have this, but it was a good coincidence because now we have a document 5330, whilst in the list we had another document. But never mind this mistake. Mr. Praljak, this document shows that the 2nd Battalion of the 2nd Brigade took out 30 detainees on the 23rd of September, 1993. Did you know it or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of a single case, Your Honours, not a single case. This never went further than this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We might proceed more quickly with the next document because we've seen it already P 00147. 6th of April, 1992, a meeting was held in Zagreb with you, Susak, and Munivrana, and you spoke after Mr. Lucic. We have spoken about it already. You might not -- do you have any special comment on the document, because we've seen it already?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's the 6th -- sorry? Well, I've talked about it. I don't have anything to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Yes. You spoke about it. Next document, P 00466. You have spoken about this document dated 11th of September, 1992, Susak, Radic, Agotic, Lucic, and Tudjman are the attendees together with you. Manolic also attended the meeting and you spoke about the military industry. If you do not mind we can move onto another document because we've seen this one already.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything to add but to say it's not Lucic but it's Lucic, it's not the same person as Ivo Lucic. These are two different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Next document, P 00524, we've seen it already, 26th of September, National Defence Council. Mr. Mesic was there, you, Mr. Susak also. You spoke on several occasions during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We now have an order, P 01202, 18th of June, 1993 -- January, 1993. The situation in Gornji Vakuf is mentioned here and this is an order by you. Can you see? You issued the order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Five MGs -- well, it's totally regular. It's -- you can see it in films. All the Western armies have it. I don't have anything to add to this, so five MGLs -- no, I -- Your Honour, I didn't sign this document, just to make it clear. I said, Okay, fine, use my authority and we'll ask for those three pieces to be returned by Kralj Tomislav Brigade, but somebody else signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not your signature but somebody signed for you. Next document, P 01350, document by the military police of the 29th of January, 1993. It is a lengthy document that we have seen already and you answered several questions in Ljubuski during a meeting that started at 6.00 p.m. I suppose you have nothing to add to what has been said already?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 01852. It is a document about Travnik, 12th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this document, or rather, I have seen it before. They want me to come back because while I was there, the situation was much, much better than it was in my absence in terms of discipline, order, military structure, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems as though the flags were burned by the BH army police. This is said in paragraph four.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The BH army at that time had already started with an open number of provocations in Travnik which would lead to -- well, what it actually led to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will note, General Praljak, that in this document there is presence of the Mujahedin in Travnik and you showed us a video of this. Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move now to the next document, P 02043. This is a document from Mr. Pasalic, April 23rd, 1993. It is a protest sent to UNPROFOR and seemingly also to the European Union.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You seem to be challenged here. It seems that everything that is occurring is blamed on you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a low-lying liar, God rest his soul. A couple of days prior to that, he had coffee with me, he walked around East Mostar, and after I prevented 30 of his men starting shooting in western Mostar, may God rest his soul, but he is a terrible liar and a scoundrel. He knew this quite well because he walked up and down East Mostar with me in order to avoid conflicts. This is all politics. This is how politics is created, in bad faith, false politics. He drank coffee with me, he -- we had agreement with the SDA so that all of us politicians and everybody else would go out in the streets, so that people would be assured that there would be no conflict, and then he turns around and writes this. He's a scoundrel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 02280. You issued this document. It is sent to Colonel Siljeg. We don't know the date exactly. Maybe you could help us with that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't be able to assist you with this document because this is not my document, and I'm saying this for the umpteenth time and I will repeat it now. This is not my handwriting, this is not my signature, this is not my style, and this is not my document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've already seen this document anyway. Next document, P 03682. This is also a document that we have already seen so we will be brief. It's when you take your post again in July you write to Mr. Tudjman asking for reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document. I signed it. I asked exactly what is written in this document, I asked for that, and I received nothing. And I repeated this again on the 5th of November in Split when I was explaining that I was leaving and how things need to be arranged after that. I spoke once again about two battalions which is proof enough that I had not received this or anything else later on, to my knowledge. Croatian army didn't come. Some volunteers came. And once again, this is evidence that had I had the brigades of the Croatian army I wouldn't have asked for these miserable battalions. You know what these battalions were like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 03821. This comes from the 4th Battalion, Petar Kresimir, July 30th, 1993, six days after you took up your post. This is a report and you're mentioned in the first paragraph. And then at the end of the document the Paraga is mentioned, the extreme Muslim. Do you know this document and what purpose does it serve in your defence case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the significance of this document is quite simple. This is a professional battalion of the HVO that heeded me none whatsoever. So a small-time commander, Vucica, who had I don't know how many soldiers under his command, simply says that I'm a fool who doesn't know what he has in the command. He has one information at his disposal and is providing other information and then he simply listened to that, and once he concluded how many soldiers he under him, he said he wouldn't listen to this fool of Praljak. He went back home and sent a report to his brigade commander. This is what the army is all about, very simply. And if you ask me what I could have done to him, I couldn't do anything. It would have taken me a month to replace him, to find somebody else instead of him because, of course, he was protected by his people down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 06203. P 06203. This is a document of October 28, 1993. You're still at your post. Colonel Siljeg is writing to the head of -- to the chief of defence department health section. We have already seen this document. Do you have any additional comments to make?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no supplemental comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 02039. This is a document of April 22nd, 1993, on the situation in Jablanica and Konjic, sent to the Main Staff of HVO in Mostar. This is a traditional report. Any comments on this one?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever. This document was created at the time when I held no office, I have no comments, except that I am familiar quite a bit with what was going on, but it's not up to me to comment on the events. I can if you wish me to, but it was sent to the Main Staff of the HVO in Mostar and at that time it was General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a small problem here, General Praljak. You are listed as being a recipient of this document. Just take a look at the end of the document. Registrar, please, could we scroll down to the last page. There further --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it. At the time I definitely did not receive this document, but since I was generally about the area at the time, probably somebody wanted me to look at what was actually going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 03957. We have already seen this document. You did not sign it but someone signed it on your behalf. It deals with Kapular and Tole. Any additional comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kapular was born in a village near Capljina. Zarko Tole was born in a village near Siroki Brijeg. Zarko Tole was a member of the HV -- or rather, he was arrested in 1992 in Bugojno. He was a member of the HVO. He had been betrayed, and then he was taken to Republika Srpska and he spent a year in prison. And then he was in the HV, HV, and here I asked for these two officers to be sent to me. Tole came, Kapular showed up and he was with the volunteers from the 9th -- from the 5th Guards Brigade with about 200 people, 140 infantrymen, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is under seal, it is P 04272. It shall not be broadcast. This is a regular report on the events in Mostar, Travnik, Tuzla, humanitarian problems, et cetera. What is the purpose of this document for your Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the idea was for the General to see item 3 on page 2. This is why this document was mentioned here, but he cannot see it on the monitor. So second page, item 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at bullet point 3. It's on the screen in your own language. It seems that there was a meeting with yourself.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was not conveyed correctly. Partially, yes. He says to defeat Muslims. I cannot defeat Muslims. I can only defend myself from the ABiH army attack. This is silly. And then that I would block the supply of the humanitarian aid. This was complete nonsense. This had never occurred to me and you could see that this was simply added. As for the water-supply, this is a complete nonsense. I don't know what these people had in their heads. Those places, Vakuf, and so on, could not be blocked, could not be cut off. I don't even know where the water source is. So each town has its own water source that they use for water-supply, for drinking water and so on, so each town does. Rama has its own source, Vakuf has its own. This is complete nonsense. I guess they read this somewhere that the water would be blocked, water-supply in San Francisco or elsewhere. I don't know. This is complete nonsense. It is true that political talks were such that we would give up Tuzla, Zepce, Vares, if an agreement would be reached. They were not part of Croatian territory that had already been agreed, but the Croats were to be protected there just as Muslims were to be protected in an area where the Croats would have majority in democratic voting and nothing else other than that. Naturally this corridor leading to the coast -- what corridor? If they want a joint state -- well, look at how absurd this is. They discuss a joint state and they want a corridor to the coast. Then whose state is it? This means they wanted to take their part and kick us out. A corridor from Paris to the coast through France to some special Frenchmen -- come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 04640. This is a document signed by you. It is sent to Mr. Marko Stanic and it's about Klis. So what's the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in an organised army one cannot write this immediately, unconditionally, and so on. When an order is written in an army, this implicitly means this is unconditional and so on, and here they add all these words. Afterwards I threatened them, I said that they need to arrest them, to keep them without water and food until I arrived because I wasn't going to carry out this order. There is a document where I say that they need to be shut up and kept without water and food until I arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document should be linked with this one; it's document P 04645. It comes from Bozo Pavlovic. It is sent to the forward command in Citluk, August 31st, 1993. This is about the Klis Independent Battalion. Comments, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't carry out the order, but they say in this document, It has been agreed orally. It's on the 1st of September that they were to take over duties -- well, listen, they're not duties in the army. This language by itself -- what do we mean when we say "army"? I keep repeating that a lot of these guys, a lot of these guys fought bravely and honourably but that there was a lot of this stuff as well, where they say conditionally we have agreed we will take over duties regarding an excursion that we are going to make and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 05188. This is a document you signed. There is no date on it. You say that this is an order from the president of HR-HB. This is sent to all units. What can you say about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. On the basis of the military chain of command, once I received an order from Mate Boban, it was my duty to convey that order to the lower echelons, to the command of operation zones that -- and the brigades they were to receive assistance, and then it says that on the basis of this order, military police and other officials need to receive written instructions, they need to receive specific tasks. And these instructions were to be explained to them. This was another attempt to introduce order, as far as I can remember, and this was an order from Mate Boban. It had to do with ensuring order in the territory, security for convoys, and so on. We should go back to the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. You indicated that the document doesn't have a date, but I was just looking at the original-language version and so the date was just omitted from the translation. It's 18th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Stringer. So the date is in the original but not in the translation, September 18, 1993. Do you agree with this, Mr. Praljak ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. With 99 per cent certainty. After a secret agreement was signed between Izetbegovic and Tudjman this order came, and at the same time they started an offensive -- actually, they started it several days prior to that. And we were to act as though nothing had happened, as though we were fools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 05279. This is a document signed by you, sent to all operational areas, and dealing with the disciplinary detention and prison sentences that could be imposed either by a commander or a person authorised by law, and there is mention of the Dretelj prison. What's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given my comment and I will add this. On the 22nd of September, everything I had in my head, all the information I had, are clearly expressed here. It was about the prison. I was sending people to the prison and I said that all the soldiers that had been punished were to be sent to Dretelj. That's what I know about what Dretelj was. And that's because maybe they had a small prison in some town and then they would release the people that were kept there, they were their friends or relatives, you know how it goes. And in order to prevent the soldiers from complaining, soldiers going to the front line who would say, Well, you punished those people and instead of being in prison they are just walking around, I issued this order that they were all to go to Dretelj and they were to be accompanied with papers indicating what they had committed, what kind of a crime, why they were sentenced to a prison term, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P 0724 -- 05724. This is a document from the Republic of Croatia, Osijek Military District, 5th Brigade of the Guards, sent to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any comments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that from the 5th Guards Brigade, from Vinkovci, there were volunteers fighting in the field under the HVO command. In a document where I list the units, some 20 of them, it is said that there is 140-something people from that unit and they were infantry men. There was some maybe 30 to 40 additional ones in -- performing other duties, and they were all volunteers. As I have explained, these volunteers are people who earlier on had left the poor areas of Herzegovina and went to fertile lands in Slavonia and so on, but they remained loyal to their old region and this is why they applied to fight as volunteers. So either they were born or their parents were born in the territory of Herzegovina, mostly in the western Herzegovina region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the next document. It is two orders requisitioning --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I don't want to waste time, but this document, P 06442, is a document we included here by error -- yes. At the time we included it based on the old description in e-court, and later on that description was changed and the document itself was changed. Therefore, we're not interested in this document. It was included erroneously on the basis of the then-existing description. When that description was corrected later on, we were not interested in this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we'll withdraw it, and move to the next one, P 08765. This is an interview given by you and it says: "I'm not responsible." Please don't give us a lengthy comment of this interview. Could you tell us why you wanted to give this interview at that point in time, May 9, 1997.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, we and Nebojsa Taraba, if you read what he claims here, what he claims, this in his introductory part, it will be clear to you that there existed an all-out campaign and that all of us were exposed to it and there was some -- it was a media campaign of the old regime. And according to them we were all thieves, criminals, and I don't know whatnot. And this text is full of lies. There are some parts that are true, and then the titles and headlines are wrong. They are attributing things to me that I didn't say and all these claims in the beginning are simply shameful. And this campaign against us, this witch-hunt was of such magnitude that to some extent I was happy when I came to face this Court so that finally you could establish what was the source of my guilt because one couldn't take this any longer. It's difficult to be in prison, it's difficult to read an indictment against yourself, but finally give me, show me a document indicating am I and why; and if so why I'm guilty. This situation where everybody can spit at you and write against you anything they want, which is a normal thing in Croatian journalism, and you cannot do anything to that person back is something that is unhealthy for your own mental health and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would like only to ask you if you have any other article or articles in the Croatian press of that time which in a way substantiate your claim and your position that this very article which we are talking about that is "nisam odgovoran" and was only an exception to the rule and you -- and your behaviour and, of course, the behaviour of the HVO was in general reflected as a positive one in some of the other publications, other articles published in Croatia during this very time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Croatian journalists split into the leftists that simply continued those communist slander without any desire to prove anything, so there was one part; and then the other smaller part were people who were trying to uncover some truth. Every week somebody wrote or uttered somewhere that I had knocked down the Old Bridge. Every week some fool had a right to do that. Initially I denied those allegations and then finally I gave up because this was an avalanche aimed against me on a daily basis and I said, Well, give me a single piece of evidence. No, nobody cared about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that your answer shows that you do not have kind of written confirmation or a kind of refusal what is being now contained in that very article. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Praljak. I have exactly 12 documents left. We'll see the next one tomorrow. It is P 00742. I'll make sure the Registrar has this one prepared tomorrow when we start the hearing and we shall return to your last document tomorrow. Remind us of it tomorrow, please. At this pace I might be able to finish in 30 or 40 minutes. Who's going to start once I'm done for cross-examination by the Defence teams? Yes, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you said that we would cover snipers -- sniper incidents which took place in Mostar during my command so that we can establish with precision - it will only take us 20 minutes - what the Prosecution claimed and how it actually looked from the mathematical point of view out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed I had told you that I would have questions on the topic. I had prepared a chart. I'll try to be quick when dealing with it. So in 30 or 40 minutes I should be done. But my question is who is going to start tomorrow. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be starting tomorrow and I will be probably asking for a short break after you finish. If you're taking 45 minutes to an hour, it might be convenient; otherwise I'll start right off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perfect. So there'll be no waste of time. I wish you all a good afternoon, a good evening. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
